# My Thinking as a Farmer

I've been working this land in Quzhou for over 35 years. My children have both moved to Shijiazhuang for work, so I manage these fields mostly on my own, with a neighbor's tractor when I need it. I have 10 mu of land — flat, silty loam, decent but not rich.

The decision is straightforward: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on 9 mu. I've been doing this rotation my whole adult life and it still makes the best economic sense. The crops complement each other — wheat's deep roots improve structure for maize, and the double-cropping calendar fits the seasons here precisely.

I attended the county agricultural extension training two years ago, and I know our groundwater situation is serious. The table has dropped noticeably since I was young. So I've committed to **3 irrigations for wheat** instead of 4 — skipping the overwintering flush. It costs me maybe 20 kg/mu in yield, but I think it's the right thing to do.

For wheat, I'll plant **Jimai 22** — an improved variety I've used for six years. It handles our dry springs well and the extension station endorses it. For maize, **Zhengdan 958** hybrid, same as last five years. I know it. It performs.

I'll use **rotary tillage for wheat** to prep the seedbed properly. For summer maize I'll seed directly into the wheat stubble — saves time and moisture, and the soil doesn't need another turn.

On fertilizer, I'm being more careful than I was at 40. I over-applied nitrogen for years and got lodging problems. Now I split the wheat nitrogen: base dressing at sowing, topdress at jointing. For maize, big ear stage is when I apply the topdress.

The remaining 1 mu I keep as a vegetable garden — garlic, cabbage, beans. Traditional varieties, mostly for ourselves and to give to neighbors. I don't count on it economically.
